content: Sodium oxide is a chemical compound with the molecular formula Na₂O. It is commonly utilized in the production of ceramics and glasses. When sodium oxide reacts with water, it forms sodium hydroxide (NaOH). The alkali metal oxides, represented by the general formula M₂O (where M can be sodium, potassium, or rubidium), crystallize in a structure known as the antifluorite structure. In this arrangement, the positions of the anions and cations are reversed compared to their positions in calcium fluoride (CaF₂). In typical applications, glass contains approximately 15% sodium oxide, with the remaining components being around 70% silicon dioxide (SiO₂) and 9% calcium oxide (CaO). Sodium oxide, often referred to as soda in this context, acts as a flux, which reduces the temperature at which silica melts. This results in soda glass having a lower melting temperature compared to pure silica. Additionally, soda glass exhibits improved mechanical properties, such as a slight increase in elasticity. These changes occur because silicon dioxide reacts with sodium oxide to form sodium silicates, which have the general formula Na₂x. Sodium oxide is formed when sodium metal reacts with oxygen. Burning sodium in air produces a mixture of sodium oxide (Na₂O) and approximately 20% sodium peroxide (Na₂O₂). Pure sodium oxide can be synthesized by reacting liquid sodium with sodium nitrate (NaNO₃).
